title: Abimelech did not want to wait for God to choose him.
paragraphs: Abimelech did not want to wait for God to choose him.
That is where the horror began.
It began with a man who wanted a crown without submission.
And if we are honest… that spirit still exists today.

The story of Abimelech is not merely ancient history buried in the book of Judges. It is one of the most psychologically terrifying portraits in Scripture because it exposes what happens when a man confuses self-promotion with divine appointment.
Judges 9 feels almost cinematic in its darkness. Blood. Manipulation. Betrayal. Political propaganda. Fear. Ego. Murder between brothers. And hovering over all of it is one chilling question:
What happens when someone crowns themselves before Heaven crowns them?
The name “Abimelech” itself is deeply revealing.
But Gideon — Abimelech’s father — was never supposed to establish a royal dynasty.
After Gideon defeated Midian, Israel begged him to rule over them.
“Rule over us—you, your son, and your grandson.”
But Gideon answered with one of the most important statements in the entire book of Judges:
“I will not rule over you, nor shall my son rule over you; the LORD shall rule over you.” — Judges 8:23
Gideon understood something Abimelech never did:
Kingship belongs to God before it belongs to men.
Israel was never meant to imitate pagan nations by grasping for power structures built on pride. Theocracy was the design. God Himself was King.
But Abimelech grew up around influence without inheriting his father’s humility.
And many people do the same today.
They inherit church culture without inheriting prayer.
They learn how to sound spiritual before learning how to surrender.
Abimelech was Gideon’s son through a concubine from Shechem. He was not the obvious heir. He was not publicly chosen. He was not spiritually confirmed. Heaven never anointed him.
“Ask all the leaders of Shechem, ‘Which is better for you: that all seventy of Jerubbaal’s sons rule over you, or that one rule over you?’ Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh.”
Because self-appointed leaders rarely seek Heaven when earthly validation is enough.
And then comes one of the darkest acts in the entire Old Testament.
“He went to his father’s house at Ophrah and killed his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone.”
Abimelech believed removing rivals would secure the throne.
But insecurity always becomes violent when identity is rooted in power.
And this is why fleshly ambition is so dangerous in spiritual spaces.
Because when someone worships position more than obedience, people become obstacles instead of souls.
Abimelech did not merely kill brothers.
And tragically, history still repeats itself.
People secretly celebrating when others fall because another person’s success feels like personal threat.
The spirit of Abimelech is still alive wherever people crave authority more than holiness.
But God never stays silent forever.
And from Mount Gerizim, Jotham delivers one of the most prophetic and poetic warnings in all Scripture.
First they approached the olive tree.
Finally they turned to the bramble.
Because truly fruitful things rarely crave domination.
Only the empty thorn bush lusted for control.
That alone should terrify every generation.
Because sometimes the people most desperate for authority are the least qualified to hold it.
“If in good faith you have acted… rejoice in Abimelech… but if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour Shechem.” — Judges 9:19-20
And that is exactly what happened.
The kingdom built through manipulation eventually consumed itself.
Because illegitimate power eventually collapses under the weight of its own corruption.
God allowed Abimelech to reign briefly.
And there is a terrifying difference between what God allows and what God approves.
“God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem.”
Because sin always carries seeds of self-destruction.
Abimelech eventually attacked a city called Thebez. During the siege, a woman dropped an upper millstone from a tower onto his head.
Judges 9:53 says the stone “crushed his skull.”
In his final moments, Abimelech begged his armor-bearer to kill him so nobody could say a woman ended his life.
Even dying, pride still controlled him.
That may be one of the saddest endings in Scripture.
A man so obsessed with image that even at death he could not face humiliation.
The man who murdered seventy brothers “on one stone” was destroyed by one stone himself.
“God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap.”
The Greek word for “mocked” is μυκτηρίζω (muktērizō).
It means “to sneer at” or “to turn up the nose in contempt.”
No one steals divine authority permanently.
Eventually crowns built by flesh collapse.
But this story is not only about Abimelech.
Because most people will never try to seize a literal throne…
but many still try to force outcomes God never ordained.
We force doors open because waiting on God feels unbearable.
But God never asked us to crown ourselves.
In the Kingdom of God, true authority flows from surrender, not self-exaltation.
Jesus did not seize authority through violence.
And because of that, God exalted Him.
One destroyed brothers to gain a crown.
The other died for His brothers to give them eternal life.
And only one Kingdom remains forever.
Maybe that is why the story still cuts so deeply.
Because somewhere inside us is a terrified human instinct that fears obscurity.
But the Kingdom of God operates upside down.
The hidden are seen by Heaven.
God is not searching for self-crowned people.
He is searching for surrendered people.
People willing to obey even when nobody applauds.
People willing to serve without titles.
People willing to wait without forcing outcomes.
People willing to decrease so Christ increases.
And maybe you needed this reminder today:
If God truly called you, you do not have to manipulate your way into destiny.
You do not have to destroy people to become somebody.
You do not have to force recognition.
You do not have to build a throne out of insecurity.
And maybe the most dangerous thing in modern Christianity is not open rebellion…
but hidden ambition wearing spiritual language.
Have you been striving more than surrendering?
Pretending to be spiritually healthy while privately exhausted?
Somebody around you is secretly collapsing under the pressure of trying to become what only God can appoint.
Some crowns are actually curses disguised as success.
